name: Bernoulli
convention: X takes the value 1 (success) with probability p and the value 0 (failure) with probability 1 − p.
limits: p = 0 and p = 1 give point masses at 0 and at 1.
Bernoulli(p) is Binomial(1, p).
A categorical law with 2 labels is 1 + X with X ~ Bernoulli(p_2).

moments.existence: All moments exist: E[X^r] = p for every r ≥ 1. The MGF exists for all real t.

links.relation: special case: Binomial(1, p)
relabelled case: a categorical law with 2 labels

name: Binomial
convention: X counts the successes in n independent trials. Each trial has the same success probability p.
limits: n = 1 gives the Bernoulli law.
If n → ∞ and np → λ, the law converges to Poisson(λ): the law of small numbers.
If n → ∞ with p fixed in (0, 1), (X − np)/√(np(1 − p)) converges in law to the standard normal law (de Moivre–Laplace).
Hypergeometric(N, K, n) converges to Binomial(n, p) as N → ∞ with K/N → p.
Each component of a multinomial count vector has a binomial law.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for all real t.

links.relation: special case n = 1
limit: n → ∞ with np → λ
limit of the hypergeometric law as N → ∞ with K/N → p
each multinomial component, and the case k = 2
the standardised count converges to N(0, 1) (de Moivre–Laplace)
the beta law is the conjugate prior of p

name: Categorical
convention: X takes the label j ∈ {1, …, k} with probability p_j. The labels are names. Their order and their values as numbers are a convention, so the CDF and the mean depend on the labels.
limits: k = 1 gives a point mass.
k = 2 gives a relabelled Bernoulli law.
Equal weights p_j = 1/k give the discrete uniform law on 1, …, k.
The indicator vector of one categorical draw is Multinomial(1, p).

moments.existence: All moments exist, because the support is finite. They depend on the labels.

links.relation: the case k = 2, relabelled
Multinomial(1, p) is the indicator vector of one draw
equal weights
an empirical law of the labels 1 … k

name: Multinomial
convention: X = (X_1, …, X_k) counts the draws in each of k categories after n categorical trials that are independent, with probabilities p.
pmf: \mathbb{P}(X = x) = \frac{n!}{x_1! \cdots x_k!} \prod_{j=1}^{k} p_j^{x_j}, \quad x_j \ge 0, \ \textstyle\sum_j x_j = n
limits: Each component has the law X_j ~ Binomial(n, p_j).
k = 2 gives (X_1, n − X_1) with X_1 ~ Binomial(n, p_1).
n = 1 gives the indicator vector of one categorical draw.
As n → ∞, (X − np)/√n converges in law to a multivariate normal law with covariance diag(p) − pp^T.

moments.variance: \operatorname{Var}(X_j) = n p_j (1 - p_j), \quad \operatorname{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = -n p_i p_j \ (i \ne j)
moments.existence: All moments exist. The components have a negative covariance, because they share the fixed total n.

links.relation: each component, and the case k = 2
the case n = 1
the standardised count vector converges to a normal law with the singular covariance diag(p) − ppᵀ. Any k − 1 components converge to a multivariate normal law of this page (all p_j > 0)
the Dirichlet law is the conjugate prior of the category probabilities

name: Discrete uniform
convention: X takes each integer from a to b with the same probability 1/m, with m = b − a + 1.
pmf: \mathbb{P}(X = k) = \frac{1}{b - a + 1}, \quad k = a, a + 1, \dots, b
limits: a = b gives a point mass.
The Zipf law with s = 0 on 1, …, N is the discrete uniform law on 1, …, N.
(X − a)/m converges in law to the continuous uniform law U(0, 1) as m → ∞.
The sum of 2 discrete uniform values that are independent has a triangular PMF, not a uniform one.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because the support is finite.

links.relation: a categorical law with equal weights, relabelled
the Zipf law with s = 0
the limit of (X − a)/m, and ⌊a + (b − a + 1)U⌋ of a continuous uniform value

name: Geometric
convention: X counts the failures before the first success in independent trials with success probability p. The other convention counts the trials, Y = X + 1 on {1, 2, …}.
limits: p = 1 gives a point mass at 0.
The geometric law is the negative binomial law with r = 1.
pX converges in law to Exponential(1) as p → 0.
It is the only law on {0, 1, 2, …} without memory: P(X ≥ s + t | X ≥ s) = P(X ≥ t).

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for t < −log(1 − p).

links.relation: special case r = 1
⌊E⌋ of an exponential value E, and pX converges to Exponential(1) as p → 0
geometric terms give the Pólya–Aeppli law
truncated below, it is a shifted geometric law

name: Negative binomial
convention: X counts the failures before success number r in independent trials with success probability p. A real r > 0 gives the gamma–Poisson mixture: Λ has a gamma law with shape r and scale (1 − p)/p, and X | Λ ~ Poisson(Λ).
limits: r = 1 gives the geometric law.
For an integer r, X is the sum of r geometric values that are independent.
If r → ∞ with the mean μ = r(1 − p)/p fixed, the law converges to Poisson(μ).
With the mean μ, the variance is μ + μ²/r. Thus the law shows overdispersion: its variance is larger than its mean.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for t < −log(1 − p).

links.relation: special case r = 1
limit: r → ∞ with the mean fixed
a Poisson count with a gamma rate is negative binomial
the negative binomial law is a gamma mixture of Poisson laws, and a finite mixture is the discrete form of it

name: Poisson
convention: X counts events. The parameter λ is the mean count.
limits: λ = 0 gives a point mass at 0.
Binomial(n, λ/n) converges to Poisson(λ) as n → ∞.
The negative binomial law with mean λ converges to Poisson(λ) as r → ∞.
The sum of independent Poisson(λ_1) and Poisson(λ_2) values has the law Poisson(λ_1 + λ_2).
(X − λ)/√λ converges in law to the standard normal law as λ → ∞.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for all real t.

links.relation: limit of Binomial(n, λ/n)
limit of the negative binomial law as r → ∞
the standardised count converges to N(0, 1) as λ → ∞
the times between the events of a Poisson process are exponential
P(N(t) < k) = P(Erlang(k, λ) > t)
a finite mixture of Poisson laws, with a variance above its mean
the number of terms of a compound Poisson sum
the zero-truncated Poisson law

name: Hypergeometric
convention: X counts the success items in n draws without replacement from N items, of which K are success items.
pmf: \mathbb{P}(X = k) = \frac{\binom{K}{k} \binom{N-K}{n-k}}{\binom{N}{n}}, \quad \max(0, n + K - N) \le k \le \min(n, K)
limits: n = N gives a point mass at K.
As N → ∞ with K/N → p, the law converges to Binomial(n, p).
The variance is the binomial variance times the finite population correction (N − n)/(N − 1).

moments.existence: All moments exist, because the support is finite.

transforms.pgf: G(z) = \textstyle\sum_k \mathbb{P}(X = k)\, z^k, \ \text{a polynomial of degree} \min(n, K)

links.relation: limit: N → ∞ with K/N → p

name: Zipf and zeta
convention: X is a rank from 1 to N with a probability proportional to k^(−s). N = ∞ gives the zeta law, which needs s > 1.
limits: s = 0 gives the discrete uniform law on 1, …, N.
N → ∞ with s > 1 gives the zeta law.
The zeta law has a regularly varying tail: P(X > k) ~ k^(1 − s)/((s − 1)ζ(s)) as k → ∞.

moments.existence: For a finite N, all moments exist. For the zeta law, E[X^r] is finite if and only if r < s − 1. Thus the mean is infinite for s ≤ 2 and the variance is infinite for s ≤ 3. The MGF of the zeta law is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: the case s = 0
the zeta sampler rejects from ⌊X⌋ with X ~ Pareto I(1, s − 1)

name: Continuous uniform
convention: X takes a value in [a, b], and intervals of equal length inside [a, b] have equal probability.
limits: a = 0 and b = 1 give the standard uniform law U(0, 1), the input of every sampler of this page.
If U ~ U(0, 1), then −log(U)/λ has the exponential law with rate λ, and log(U/(1 − U)) has the standard logistic law.
For integers a ≤ b, ⌊a + (b − a + 1)U⌋ has the discrete uniform law on {a, …, b}.
The sum of n independent U(0, 1) values has the Irwin–Hall law. For a large n it is near the normal law with mean n/2 and variance n/12.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because the support is bounded. The MGF exists for all real t.

links.relation: U(0, 1) is Beta(1, 1)
−log(U)/λ is exponential: the inverse transform
log(U/(1 − U)) is standard logistic
the discrete version: ⌊a + (b − a + 1)U⌋
the GPD with ξ = −1 is uniform on [μ, μ + σ]

name: Normal
convention: X has the mean μ and the standard deviation σ. The density is symmetric about μ.
limits: σ → 0 gives the point mass at μ.
The central limit theorem: a normalised sum of i.i.d. values with a finite, positive variance converges in law to N(0, 1).
Binomial(n, p) is near N(np, np(1 − p)) for a large n (de Moivre–Laplace), and Poisson(λ) is near N(λ, λ) for a large λ.
Student's t law with ν degrees of freedom converges to N(0, 1) as ν → ∞.
If Z ~ N(0, 1), then Z² has the chi-square law with 1 degree of freedom.
Each component of a multivariate normal vector is normal.
A normal law whose variance is exponential gives the Laplace law.

moments.existence: All moments exist. P(|X − μ| > kσ) is about 0.317, 0.0455 and 0.0027 for k = 1, 2 and 3. The MGF exists for all real t.

links.relation: each component of a multivariate normal vector
the limit of Student's t law as ν → ∞
Z² is χ²(1), and a sum of ν squared independent N(0, 1) values is χ²(ν)
the limit of the standardised binomial law (de Moivre–Laplace)
the limit of the standardised Poisson law as λ → ∞
a normal law with an exponential variance is Laplace
exp(X) is lognormal
the ratio of two independent standard normal values is Cauchy
μ + c/Z² is Lévy for a standard normal Z
the stable law with α = 2 is N(δ, 2γ²)
a finite mixture of normal laws
the kernel of the kernel density model

name: Multivariate normal
convention: X = (X₁, …, X_k) has the mean vector μ and the covariance matrix Σ, which is symmetric and positive definite. The model text writes Σ as k² entries, row by row.
limits: k = 1 gives the normal law N(μ, Σ₁₁).
Each component X_j is N(μ_j, Σ_jj). Each linear form a + bᵀX is normal, with the mean a + bᵀμ and the variance bᵀΣb.
Components with covariance 0 are independent, because the vector is jointly normal. For other laws, covariance 0 does not imply independence in general.
X = μ + LZ, with L the Cholesky factor of Σ and Z a vector of independent N(0, 1) values.
For |ρ| < 1 the joint tails are asymptotically independent: the normal law has no tail dependence. Group 5 adds copulas with tail dependence.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The page reads the vector through its components X[j], their sums and their linear forms.

links.relation: each component and each linear form is normal
the limit of the standardised multinomial count vector, a degenerate normal law with the singular covariance diag(p) − ppᵀ. Any k − 1 components have a positive definite limit

name: Exponential
convention: X is a waiting time with a constant rate λ: P(X > t) = e^(−λt). The mean is 1/λ.
limits: Memorylessness: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t). It is the only continuous law with this property.
Exponential(λ) is Gamma(1, 1/λ) and Erlang(1, λ).
The times between the events of a Poisson process with rate λ are i.i.d. Exponential(λ). Thus the count of events in [0, t] is Poisson(λt).
⌊X⌋ has the geometric law with the success probability 1 − e^(−λ).
The minimum of independent exponential values with rates λ_i is exponential with the rate Σλ_i.
The difference of two i.i.d. exponential values has the Laplace law.
χ²(2) is the exponential law with rate 1/2.

moments.existence: All moments exist: E[X^r] = r!/λ^r. The MGF exists for t < λ.

links.relation: the special case k = 1, θ = 1/λ
the special case k = 1
⌊X⌋ is geometric with p = 1 − e^(−λ)
the waiting times of a Poisson process
the difference of two i.i.d. exponential values is Laplace
−log(U)/λ for U ~ U(0, 1)
χ²(2) is exponential with rate 1/2
the Weibull law with k = 1
the limit of the Gompertz law as b → 0 with ηb fixed
log(X/x_m) of a Pareto I value
the law of the waiting time given its rate, in the gamma mixture that gives the Pareto II law
the GPD with ξ = 0
the maximum of n exponential values minus log n tends to the Gumbel law
a common law of censoring times

name: Gamma
convention: X has the shape k and the scale θ, so its mean is kθ. For an integer k it is the sum of k independent exponential values with mean θ.
limits: k = 1 gives the exponential law with rate 1/θ.
An integer k gives the Erlang law: Erlang(k, λ) = Gamma(k, 1/λ).
Gamma(ν/2, 2) is the chi-square law with ν degrees of freedom.
For independent values with the same scale, Gamma(k₁, θ) + Gamma(k₂, θ) = Gamma(k₁ + k₂, θ).
As k → ∞, (X − kθ)/(θ√k) converges in law to N(0, 1).
If G₁ ~ Gamma(a, 1) and G₂ ~ Gamma(b, 1) are independent, then G₁/(G₁ + G₂) ~ Beta(a, b). Normalised gamma values give the Dirichlet law.
A Poisson count whose rate has a gamma law has the negative binomial law.

moments.existence: All moments exist: E[X^r] = θ^r Γ(k + r)/Γ(k). The density is unbounded at 0 for k < 1. The MGF exists for t < 1/θ.

links.relation: the special case k = 1
an integer shape: Erlang(k, λ) = Gamma(k, 1/λ)
χ²(ν) = Gamma(ν/2, 2)
G₁/(G₁ + G₂) is beta
normalised gamma values are Dirichlet
a gamma mixture of Poisson laws is negative binomial
the law of the rate in an exponential–gamma mixture, which gives the Pareto II law

name: Erlang
convention: X is the sum of k independent exponential phases, each with rate λ: the time of the k-th event of a Poisson process with rate λ.
limits: k = 1 gives the exponential law.
Erlang(k, λ) = Gamma(k, 1/λ).
P(X > t) = P(N(t) < k) = Σ_{j<k} e^(−λt)(λt)^j/j!, with N(t) ~ Poisson(λt).
As k → ∞ with the mean k/λ fixed, X converges to the constant k/λ: the coefficient of variation is 1/√k.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for t < λ.

links.relation: the special case k = 1, and the law of each phase
Erlang(k, λ) = Gamma(k, 1/λ)
P(X > t) = P(N(t) < k) for a Poisson process

name: Beta
convention: X is a proportion in [0, 1] with the shapes a and b. The mean is a/(a + b).
limits: a < 1 and b < 1 give a U shape. a = b gives a law that is symmetric about 1/2.
G₁/(G₁ + G₂) with independent G₁ ~ Gamma(a, 1) and G₂ ~ Gamma(b, 1).
Each component of a Dirichlet vector is beta, and the Dirichlet law with 2 parts is the beta law.
Beta(a, b) is the conjugate prior of a binomial success probability. After k successes in n trials, the posterior is Beta(a + k, b + n − k).
If Y ~ Beta(d₁/2, d₂/2), then d₂Y/(d₁(1 − Y)) has the F(d₁, d₂) law.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because the support is bounded. The density is unbounded at 0 for a < 1 and at 1 for b < 1.

links.relation: Beta(1, 1) is U(0, 1)
G₁/(G₁ + G₂) of independent gamma values
the case k = 2, and each component
the conjugate prior of the success probability
d₂Y/(d₁(1 − Y)) is F(d₁, d₂)

name: Dirichlet
convention: X = (X₁, …, X_k) is a vector of proportions with X_j ≥ 0 and Σ X_j = 1. The concentrations α_j set the means α_j/α₀, with α₀ = Σ α_j. At fixed means, a larger α₀ gives a smaller spread: Var X_j = m_j(1 − m_j)/(α₀ + 1), with m_j = α_j/α₀.
limits: k = 2 gives the beta law: X₁ ~ Beta(α₁, α₂).
Each component X_j ~ Beta(α_j, α₀ − α_j).
X_j = G_j/Σ G_i, with independent G_j ~ Gamma(α_j, 1).
It is the conjugate prior of multinomial probabilities: after the counts n_j, the posterior is Dirichlet(α_j + n_j).
α_j = 1 for every j gives the uniform law on the simplex.

moments.existence: All moments exist, because each component is in [0, 1].

transforms.mgf: M(t) = \mathbb{E}\,e^{t^{\top}X} \ \text{is finite for every} \ t \in \mathbb{R}^k \ \text{(no closed form)}

links.relation: each component, and the case k = 2
normalised independent gamma values
the conjugate prior of the category probabilities

name: Chi-square
convention: X is the sum of ν squared independent standard normal values. A real ν > 0 gives Gamma(ν/2, 2).
limits: χ²(ν) = Gamma(ν/2, 2).
χ²(2) is the exponential law with rate 1/2.
(X − ν)/√(2ν) converges in law to N(0, 1) as ν → ∞. The right tail converges slowly.
For n i.i.d. normal values with variance σ², (n − 1)S²/σ² ~ χ²(n − 1).
Z/√(V/ν), with Z ~ N(0, 1) and V ~ χ²(ν) independent, has Student's t law.
(V₁/d₁)/(V₂/d₂), with independent chi-square values, has the F law.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for t < 1/2.

links.relation: the sum of ν squared standard normal values
χ²(ν) = Gamma(ν/2, 2)
ν = 2 gives the exponential law with rate 1/2
V in T = Z/√(V/ν)
the ratio of two scaled chi-square values is F

name: Student's t
convention: T = Z/√(V/ν), with Z ~ N(0, 1) and V ~ χ²(ν) independent. The page uses the standard t law: write μ + sT for a location μ and a scale s.
limits: ν = 1 gives the Cauchy law, which has no mean.
ν → ∞ gives N(0, 1).
T² ~ F(1, ν).
The tail is regularly varying: P(T > t) ~ c t^(−ν) as t → ∞.
T is a scale mixture of normal laws: T = Z/√W with νW ~ χ²(ν).

moments.existence: E|T|^r is finite if and only if r < ν. Thus the mean exists only for ν > 1, and the variance only for ν > 2. The MGF is infinite for every t ≠ 0.

links.relation: the limit as ν → ∞, and Z in Z/√(V/ν)
V in Z/√(V/ν)
T² ~ F(1, ν)
the case ν = 1

name: F (Fisher–Snedecor)
convention: X = (V₁/d₁)/(V₂/d₂), with independent V₁ ~ χ²(d₁) and V₂ ~ χ²(d₂): the ratio of two variance estimates.
limits: T² ~ F(1, ν) for Student's T with ν degrees of freedom.
d₁X converges in law to χ²(d₁) as d₂ → ∞.
1/X ~ F(d₂, d₁).
d₁X/(d₁X + d₂) ~ Beta(d₁/2, d₂/2).
The right tail is regularly varying with index d₂/2.

moments.existence: E[X^r] is finite if and only if r < d₂/2. Thus the mean needs d₂ > 2, and the variance needs d₂ > 4. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: the ratio of two scaled chi-square values
T² ~ F(1, ν)
d₁X/(d₁X + d₂) is Beta(d₁/2, d₂/2)

name: Logistic
convention: X has the location μ and the scale s. Its CDF is the logistic (sigmoid) function of (x − μ)/s.
limits: The CDF is the inverse of the logit function log(p/(1 − p)).
log(U/(1 − U)) for U ~ U(0, 1) is standard logistic.
The difference of two i.i.d. standard Gumbel values is standard logistic.
The variance is s²π²/3. At the same variance its tails are heavier than normal tails: P(X > μ + 3σ) is about 0.0043, against 0.00135 for the normal law.
A logistic latent variable gives the logit model of a binary response, and the Elo model of a game.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for |t| < 1/s.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = e^{\mu t}\,\frac{\pi s t}{\sin(\pi s t)}, \quad |t| < 1/s
transforms.cf: \varphi(t) = e^{i\mu t}\,\frac{\pi s t}{\sinh(\pi s t)}

links.relation: log(U/(1 − U)) of a uniform value
each is the rejection proposal of the other, with M = 2
exp(X) is log-logistic

name: Laplace
convention: X has the location μ and the scale b: a symmetric law with a sharp peak at μ and exponential tails, P(|X − μ| > t) = e^(−t/b).
limits: The difference of two i.i.d. exponential values with mean b is Laplace(0, b).
|X − μ| is exponential with mean b.
A normal law whose variance is exponential gives the Laplace law: a scale mixture.
The median of a sample is the maximum likelihood estimate of μ, as the mean is for the normal law.
The Laplace mechanism of differential privacy adds Laplace(0, Δ/ε) noise to a statistic with sensitivity Δ.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for |t| < 1/b.

links.relation: the difference of two i.i.d. exponential values, and |X − μ| is exponential
a scale mixture of normal laws with an exponential variance
each is the rejection proposal of the other, with M = 2

name: Lognormal
convention: X = exp(μ + σZ), with Z ~ N(0, 1). Thus log X ~ N(μ, σ²). The median is e^μ, and σ is the standard deviation of log X.
limits: σ → 0 gives the point mass at e^μ.
The product of independent lognormal values is lognormal: the values of μ add, and the values of σ² add.
X^a is lognormal with the parameters aμ and |a|σ for a ≠ 0. Thus 1/X is lognormal with −μ and σ.
The tail is subexponential but not regularly varying. P(X > x) decreases faster than every power of x and more slowly than every exponential function.
The moments do not identify the law: other laws have the same moments E[X^r] for all integers r (Heyde 1963).

moments.existence: All moments exist: E[X^r] = exp(rμ + r²σ²/2) for every real r. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0. The Laplace transform E[e^(−sX)] is finite for s ≥ 0 but has no closed form.

links.relation: log X ~ N(μ, σ²)
another subexponential lifetime law when k < 1. All moments are finite in both laws
a competing positive law: the experiment of the inverse Gaussian law compares two laws with the same mean and variance
lognormal lifetimes under censoring

name: Weibull
convention: X has the shape k and the scale λ: P(X > x) = exp(−(x/λ)^k). The hazard k x^(k−1)/λ^k decreases for k < 1, is constant for k = 1 and increases for k > 1.
limits: k = 1 gives the exponential law with the rate 1/λ.
k = 2 gives the Rayleigh law with the scale λ/√2.
(X/λ)^k is standard exponential.
The minimum of n independent Weibull(k, λ) values is Weibull(k, λn^(−1/k)): the weakest-link property.
k → ∞ gives the point mass at λ.
For k < 1 the tail is subexponential, but all moments are finite.

moments.existence: All moments exist: E[X^r] = λ^r Γ(1 + r/k) for r > −k. The MGF is finite for every t when k > 1, and for t < 1/λ when k = 1. It is infinite for every t > 0 when k < 1.

links.relation: the case k = 1, with the rate 1/λ
−X is reverse Weibull with the same shape
1/X is Fréchet with the shape k and the scale 1/λ
another positive lifetime law. The lognormal tail is heavier than every Weibull tail
Burr XII(c, k, λk^(1/c)) tends to Weibull(c, λ) as k → ∞
another parametric hazard: a power of x against an exponential function of x
−k·log(X/λ) is standard Gumbel
Weibull lifetimes under censoring

name: Inverse Gaussian
convention: X has the mean μ and the shape λ. Let a Brownian motion have the drift ν > 0 and the variance σ² per unit time. The time at which it first reaches the level a > 0 is IG(μ, λ), with μ = a/ν and λ = a²/σ².
limits: The sum of n independent IG(μ, λ) values is IG(nμ, n²λ). Thus the sample mean is IG(μ, nλ).
μ → ∞ gives the Lévy law with the location 0 and the scale λ: the first-passage time of a Brownian motion with no drift.
λ → ∞ gives the point mass at μ, and (X − μ)/√(μ³/λ) tends to N(0, 1).
cX is IG(cμ, cλ) for c > 0.
λ(X − μ)²/(μ²X) has the χ²(1) law.
The tail decreases as x^(−3/2) e^(−λx/(2μ²)): an exponential tail.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF is finite for t ≤ λ/(2μ²) and infinite for t > λ/(2μ²).

links.relation: a competing positive law: with the same mean and variance, the lognormal law has the heavier tail
IG(μ, λ) tends to Lévy(0, λ) as μ → ∞: the first-passage time of a Brownian motion with no drift

name: Gompertz
convention: X has the hazard ηb·e^(bx): it starts at ηb and grows by the factor e^b in each unit of time. P(X > x) = exp(−η(e^(bx) − 1)). The hazard doubles every log(2)/b units of time.
limits: b → 0 with ηb fixed gives the exponential law with the rate ηb.
η(e^(bX) − 1) is standard exponential, so X = log(1 + E/η)/b with E ~ Exp(1).
The Gompertz law is the minimum-Gumbel law with the scale 1/b and the location log(1/η)/b, conditioned to be positive.
The mode is log(1/η)/b for η < 1, and 0 for η ≥ 1.
A constant added to the hazard gives the Gompertz–Makeham law.

moments.variance: \frac{\eta e^{\eta}}{b^2}\int_1^\infty (\log u)^2 e^{-\eta u}\,du - \left(\frac{e^{\eta} E_1(\eta)}{b}\right)^2 \ \text{(no elementary closed form)}
moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF is finite for every real t, because the tail decreases faster than every exponential function.

links.relation: the Gompertz law is the minimum-Gumbel law with the scale 1/b, conditioned to be positive
another parametric hazard: an exponential function of x against a power of x
b → 0 with ηb fixed gives the exponential law with the rate ηb

name: Log-logistic (Fisk)
convention: X has the scale α, which is the median, and the shape β. log X is logistic with the location log α and the scale 1/β. Economists call it the Fisk law.
limits: k = 1 in Burr XII(c, k, λ) gives the log-logistic law with α = λ and β = c.
β = 1 gives X/α ~ F(2, 2), which is also Pareto II with μ = 0, σ = α and the tail index 1.
β → ∞ gives the point mass at α.
The hazard β x^(β − 1)/(α^β + x^β) decreases for β ≤ 1. For β > 1 it rises to a maximum at x = α(β − 1)^(1/β) and then falls.
The tail is regularly varying: P(X > x) ~ (x/α)^(−β) as x → ∞.
For an income model, the Gini coefficient is 1/β (β > 1).

moments.existence: E[X^r] is finite if and only if −β < r < β. Thus the mean is infinite for β ≤ 1, and the variance is infinite for β ≤ 2. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: log X is logistic with location log α and scale 1/β
the case k = 1 of Burr XII, with λ = α and c = β

name: Pareto I
convention: X has the least value x_m and the tail index α: P(X > x) = (x/x_m)^(−α) for x ≥ x_m.
limits: log(X/x_m) is exponential with rate α.
Scale invariance: for t ≥ x_m, the law of X given X > t is Pareto I(t, α). Thus P(X > 2t)/P(X > t) = 2^(−α) for every t ≥ x_m.
The minimum of n independent Pareto I(x_m, α) values is Pareto I(x_m, nα).
For n independent values, max/(x_m n^(1/α)) converges in law to the Fréchet law with the shape α.
α → ∞ gives the point mass at x_m.
Pareto I(x_m, α) is Pareto II with μ = σ = x_m, and GPD with ξ = 1/α, σ = x_m/α and μ = x_m.

moments.existence: E[X^r] is finite if and only if r < α: E[X^r] = α x_m^r/(α − r). Thus the mean is infinite for α ≤ 1, and the variance is infinite for α ≤ 2. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: Pareto I(x_m, α) is Pareto II with μ = σ = x_m
GPD with ξ = 1/α, σ = x_m/α, μ = x_m
the normalised maximum of Pareto I draws tends to the Fréchet law
log(X/x_m) is exponential with rate α
rejection from ⌊X⌋ with X ~ Pareto I(1, s − 1) draws the zeta law: the page's zeta sampler

name: Pareto II (Lomax)
convention: X has the least value μ, the scale σ and the tail index α: P(X > x) = (1 + (x − μ)/σ)^(−α) for x ≥ μ. μ = 0 gives the Lomax law.
limits: Gamma mixture: if Λ ~ Gamma(α, 1/σ) and X − μ, given Λ, is exponential with rate Λ, then X ~ Pareto II(μ, σ, α).
α → ∞ with σ/α = θ fixed gives μ plus an exponential value with mean θ.
Excess over a threshold: for u ≥ μ, X − u given X > u is Pareto II(0, σ + u − μ, α). Thus the mean excess σ + u − μ over α − 1 increases linearly in u (α > 1).
μ = σ = x_m gives Pareto I(x_m, α).
The tail is regularly varying with index α. Thus the law is subexponential: P(X₁ + … + X_n > x) ~ n P(X > x) as x → ∞.

moments.existence: E|X − μ|^r is finite if and only if r < α. Thus the mean is infinite for α ≤ 1, and the variance is infinite for α ≤ 2. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: the case μ = σ = x_m is Pareto I(x_m, α)
Pareto II(μ, σ, α) is GPD with ξ = 1/α, σ_GPD = σ/α
the case c = 1 of Burr XII
an exponential value with a gamma-distributed rate
the conditional law given the rate

name: Burr XII (Singh–Maddala)
convention: X has the shapes c and k and the scale λ: P(X > x) = (1 + (x/λ)^c)^(−k). c sets the body near 0. The product ck is the tail index. Economists call it the Singh–Maddala law.
limits: k = 1 gives the log-logistic law with α = λ and β = c.
c = 1 gives Pareto II with μ = 0, σ = λ and the tail index k.
k → ∞ with λ = θk^(1/c) gives the Weibull law with the shape c and the scale θ.
(X/λ)^c is Pareto II(0, 1, k).
The tail is regularly varying: P(X > x) ~ (x/λ)^(−ck) as x → ∞.
For c < 1 the density has no bound near 0. For c > 1 the mode is λ((c − 1)/(ck + 1))^(1/c).

moments.existence: E[X^r] = λ^r k B(k − r/c, 1 + r/c) is finite if and only if −c < r < ck. Thus the mean is infinite for ck ≤ 1, and the variance is infinite for ck ≤ 2. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: the case k = 1, with α = λ and β = c
the case c = 1, with μ = 0, σ = λ and α = k
the limit k → ∞ with the scale λk^(1/c)

name: Fréchet
convention: X = m + sY, with P(Y ≤ y) = exp(−y^(−α)) for y > 0. α is the tail index, s the scale and m the least value. The Fréchet law is the GEV law with ξ = 1/α > 0.
limits: Max-stability: the maximum of n independent Fréchet(α, s, m) values has the law Fréchet(α, n^(1/α)s, m).
Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko: let P(X > x) be regularly varying with the tail index α. Then the maximum of n draws, divided by the 1 − 1/n quantile, tends in law to Fréchet(α, 1, 0).
α·log((X − m)/s) has the Gumbel law with location 0 and scale 1, for every α.
1/(X − m) has the Weibull law with shape α and scale 1/s.
The tail is regularly varying: P(X > x) ~ ((x − m)/s)^(−α) as x → ∞.

moments.existence: For r > 0, E|X|^r is finite if and only if r < α, and E[((X − m)/s)^r] = Γ(1 − r/α) for r < α. Thus the mean is infinite for α ≤ 1, and the variance is infinite for α ≤ 2. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: GEV with ξ = 1/α > 0: Fréchet(α, s, m) = GEV(μ = m + s, σ = s/α, ξ = 1/α)
1/X with X ~ Weibull(α, 1/s) is Fréchet(α, s, 0)
the limit law of the normalised maximum: the maximum of n Pareto I(x_m, α) draws over n^(1/α)x_m tends to Fréchet(α, 1, 0)

name: Cauchy
convention: X = x_0 + γ tan(π(U − 1/2)), with U uniform on (0, 1). x_0 is the median and the mode. γ is the half-width at half-maximum and half the interquartile range.
limits: x_0 = 0 and γ = 1 give Student's t law with ν = 1.
Z_1/Z_2, with Z_1 and Z_2 independent standard normal values, has the law Cauchy(0, 1).
The mean of n independent Cauchy(x_0, γ) values has the law Cauchy(x_0, γ) for every n. The law of large numbers does not apply.
If X ~ Cauchy(0, γ), then 1/X ~ Cauchy(0, 1/γ).
The tail is regularly varying with index 1: P(X > x) ~ γ/(πx) as x → ∞.
Cauchy(x_0, γ) is the stable law S(1, 0, γ, x_0; 0).

moments.existence: For r > 0, E|X|^r is finite if and only if r < 1. The mean does not exist, because E[max(X, 0)] and E[max(−X, 0)] are both infinite. The median x_0 and the interquartile range 2γ always exist. The MGF is infinite for every t ≠ 0.

links.relation: Cauchy(x₀, γ) is S(1, 0, γ, x₀; 0)
Student's t with ν = 1 is Cauchy(0, 1)
the ratio of two independent standard normal values is Cauchy(0, 1)

name: Lévy
convention: X = μ + c/Z², with Z standard normal. μ is the least value and c the scale. X − μ has the law of the first-passage time of a standard Brownian motion to the level √c. The CDF is F(x) = erfc(√(c/(2(x − μ)))).
limits: The first-passage time of a standard Brownian motion with no drift to the level a ≠ 0 has the law Lévy(0, a²).
IG(μ, λ) tends to Lévy(0, λ) as μ → ∞: a drift towards the level gives the inverse Gaussian law, and no drift gives the Lévy law.
The sum of n independent Lévy(μ, c) values has the law Lévy(nμ, n²c). Thus their mean has the law Lévy(μ, nc).
X − μ has the inverse gamma law with shape 1/2 and scale c/2.
The tail is regularly varying with index 1/2: P(X > x) ~ √(2c/(π(x − μ))) as x → ∞.
Lévy(μ, c) is the stable law S(1/2, 1, c, μ + c; 0). The mode is μ + c/3.

moments.existence: E[(X − μ)^r] is finite if and only if r < 1/2. Thus the mean and the variance are infinite. The median μ + c/(2 (erfc⁻¹(1/2))²) ≈ μ + 2.198c exists. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0.

links.relation: Lévy(μ, c) is S(1/2, 1, c, μ + c; 0)
Lévy(0, c) is the limit μ → ∞ of IG(μ, λ) with λ = c
μ + c/Z² with Z standard normal

name: Stable (S0)
convention: Nolan's S0 parameterisation S(α, β, γ, δ; 0): α is the index of stability, β the skewness, γ the scale and δ the location. The S0 form is continuous in all parameters. The S1 form has the location δ₁ = δ − βγ tan(πα/2) for α ≠ 1, and δ₁ = δ − (2/π)βγ log γ for α = 1. The page computes the density and the CDF by numerical integrals (Nolan 1997), so their reference values have the tag "numerical". The inverse transform uses an interpolated table of 401 quantiles of this CDF, so it is approximate. The Chambers–Mallows–Stuck method samples exactly.
pdf: f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-itx}\,\varphi(t)\,dt \ \text{(no closed form in general)}
limits: α = 2 gives N(δ, 2γ²) for every β.
α = 1 and β = 0 give Cauchy(δ, γ).
α = 1/2 and β = 1 give Lévy(δ − γ, γ).
The sum of n independent S(α, β, γ, δ; 0) values is S(α, β, n^(1/α)γ, δ_n; 0).
In the sum law, δ_n = nδ + βγ tan(πα/2)(n^(1/α) − n) for α ≠ 1, and δ_n = nδ + (2/π)βγ n log n for α = 1.

Generalised central limit theorem: let the two tails of a law be regularly varying with the tail index α, with 0 < α < 2, with a limit of their ratio. Then centred and scaled sums of i.i.d. draws tend in law to a stable law with this α.
For α < 2, P(X > x) ~ γ^α c_α (1 + β) x^(−α) as x → ∞, with c_α = Γ(α) sin(πα/2)/π.

moments.existence: For α < 2 and r > 0, E|X|^r is finite if and only if r < α. Thus the variance is infinite for α < 2, and the mean exists only for α > 1. For α = 2 all moments exist. For α < 2 and |β| < 1 the MGF is infinite for every t ≠ 0. For α < 2 and β = 1 it is finite only for t ≤ 0, and for β = −1 only for t ≥ 0.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = \infty \ \text{for every} \ t \ne 0 \ (\alpha < 2, |\beta| < 1); \quad M(t) = e^{\delta t + \gamma^2 t^2} \ (\alpha = 2)

links.relation: α = 1 and β = 0 give Cauchy(δ, γ)
α = 1/2 and β = 1 give Lévy(δ − γ, γ)
α = 2 gives N(δ, 2γ²)

name: Generalised extreme value (GEV)
convention: The GEV law with shape ξ, location μ and scale σ is the law of a normalised maximum. ξ > 0 gives the Fréchet type, with a power tail. ξ = 0 gives the Gumbel type. ξ < 0 gives the reverse Weibull type, with a finite upper end point μ − σ/ξ.
pdf: f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma}\, t(x)^{\xi+1} e^{-t(x)}, \quad t(x) = \left(1 + \xi\,\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^{-1/\xi} \ (\xi \ne 0), \quad t(x) = e^{-(x-\mu)/\sigma} \ (\xi = 0)
limits: ξ = 0 gives the Gumbel law with location μ and scale σ.
ξ = 1/α > 0 gives a Fréchet law: X = μ + σ(Y − 1)/ξ with Y ~ Fréchet(α, 1, 0).
ξ = −1/α < 0 gives a reverse Weibull law with the upper end point μ − σ/ξ.
Max-stability: the maximum of n independent GEV(ξ, μ, σ) values is GEV(ξ, μ + σ(n^ξ − 1)/ξ, σ n^ξ).
Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko: every non-degenerate limit law of a normalised maximum of i.i.d. values is a GEV law.

moments.existence: For ξ > 0 and r > 0, E|X|^r is finite if and only if r < 1/ξ: the mean needs ξ < 1 and the variance needs ξ < 1/2. For ξ ≤ 0 all moments exist. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0 when ξ > 0.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = e^{\mu t}\,\Gamma(1 - \sigma t) \ (\xi = 0, \ t < 1/\sigma); \ \text{infinite for every} \ t > 0 \ (\xi > 0)
transforms.cf: \text{no closed form for} \ \xi \ne 0; \ \varphi(t) = e^{i\mu t}\,\Gamma(1 - i\sigma t) \ (\xi = 0)

links.relation: the case ξ = 1/α > 0, after a change of location and scale
the case ξ = 0
the case ξ = −1/α < 0, after a change of location and scale
the excesses over a high threshold of a law in the domain of attraction of GEV_ξ tend to GPD_ξ

name: Generalised Pareto (GPD)
convention: X is the threshold μ plus an excess Y with P(Y > y) = (1 + ξy/σ)^(−1/ξ), for y ≥ 0 and 1 + ξy/σ > 0. For ξ = 0 this is the limit e^(−y/σ). ξ is the shape and σ > 0 is the scale. ξ > 0 gives a power tail with the index 1/ξ. ξ < 0 gives the end point μ + σ/|ξ|.
limits: ξ = 0 gives the exponential law with the mean σ, moved by μ.
ξ = −1 gives the uniform law on [μ, μ + σ].
ξ > 0 gives the Pareto II (Lomax) law with α = 1/ξ and the scale σ/ξ.
Threshold stability: for a threshold u ≥ μ below the end point, the excess X − u given X > u is GPD(ξ, σ + ξ(u − μ)).
The mean excess E[X − u | X > u] = (σ + ξ(u − μ))/(1 − ξ) is linear in u, for ξ < 1.
Pickands–Balkema–de Haan: take a law in the domain of attraction of GEV_ξ. Its excess over a threshold u, scaled suitably, tends to GPD_ξ as u tends to the upper end point.

moments.existence: For ξ > 0 and r > 0, E|X|^r is finite if and only if r < 1/ξ. Thus the mean exists only for ξ < 1, and the variance only for ξ < 1/2. For ξ ≤ 0, all moments exist. The MGF is infinite for every t > 0 when ξ > 0. It exists for t < 1/σ when ξ = 0, and for every t when ξ < 0.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = \frac{e^{\mu t}}{1 - \sigma t} \ (\xi = 0, \ t < 1/\sigma); \quad M(t) = \infty \ \text{for every} \ t > 0 \ (\xi > 0); \quad \text{no closed form for } \xi < 0 \text{ in general}
transforms.cf: \varphi(t) = \frac{e^{i\mu t}}{1 - i\sigma t} \ (\xi = 0); \quad \text{no closed form in elementary functions for } \xi \ne 0

links.relation: the excesses over a high threshold of a law in the domain of attraction of GEV_ξ tend to GPD_ξ (Pickands–Balkema–de Haan)
for ξ > 0, GPD(ξ, σ, μ) is Pareto II with α = 1/ξ, the scale σ/ξ and the location μ
Pareto I(x_m, α) is the GPD with ξ = 1/α, σ = x_m/α and μ = x_m
ξ = 0 gives μ plus an exponential value with the mean σ
ξ = −1 gives the uniform law on [μ, μ + σ]

name: Gumbel
convention: X has the Gumbel law for maxima: P(X ≤ x) = exp(−e^(−(x − μ)/β)). μ is the mode and β > 0 is the scale. This is the GEV law with ξ = 0. The Gumbel law for minima is the law of −X.
limits: Max-stability: the maximum of n i.i.d. Gumbel(μ, β) values is Gumbel(μ + β log n, β).
If E is a standard exponential value, μ − β log E is Gumbel(μ, β).
The maximum of n standard exponential values minus log n tends to the standard Gumbel law.
The maxima of normal, lognormal, gamma and Weibull values have the Gumbel law as their limit after a suitable scaling.
The difference of two i.i.d. Gumbel(μ, β) values has the logistic law with the location 0 and the scale β.
The Gumbel-max rule: if G_i are i.i.d. standard Gumbel values, the index of the largest log p_i + G_i has the categorical law with the probabilities p_i.

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for t < 1/β and is infinite for t ≥ 1/β, because the right tail is exponential.

links.relation: the GEV law with ξ = 0
if G ~ Gumbel(μ, β), then −G given −G > 0 is Gompertz with b = 1/β and η = e^(μ/β). This is the minimum-Gumbel law, conditioned to be positive
−k log(X/λ) of a Weibull(k, λ) value X is standard Gumbel
the maximum of n standard exponential values minus log n tends to the standard Gumbel law

name: Reverse Weibull
convention: X has the upper end point μ: P(X ≤ x) = exp(−((μ − x)/σ)^α) for x < μ, and 1 for x ≥ μ. α > 0 is the shape and σ > 0 is the scale. μ − X has the Weibull law with the shape α and the scale σ. This is the GEV law with ξ = −1/α < 0, written with its end point.
limits: α = 1: μ − X is exponential with the mean σ.
α = 2: μ − X has the Rayleigh law with the scale σ/√2.
The maxima of i.i.d. values with an end point x* and P(X > x* − y) ~ c y^α as y → 0 have this law as their limit. The uniform law gives α = 1, and the GPD with ξ < 0 gives α = −1/ξ.
As α → ∞, α(X − μ + σ)/σ tends to the standard Gumbel law.
Max-stability: the maximum of n i.i.d. values has the same law with the scale σ n^(−1/α).

moments.existence: All moments exist. The MGF exists for every t ≥ 0, because X ≤ μ. For t < 0 it exists for every t when α > 1, for t > −1/σ when α = 1, and for no t < 0 when α < 1.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = e^{\mu t}\,\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-t\sigma W}\right], \ W \sim \text{Weibull}(\alpha, 1): \ \text{no closed form in general}; \quad M(t) = \frac{e^{\mu t}}{1 + \sigma t} \ (\alpha = 1, \ t > -1/\sigma)
transforms.cf: \varphi(t) = e^{i\mu t}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-i\sigma t)^n}{n!}\,\Gamma\left(1 + \frac{n}{\alpha}\right) \ (\alpha > 1); \quad \varphi(t) = \frac{e^{i\mu t}}{1 + i\sigma t} \ (\alpha = 1)

links.relation: the GEV law with ξ = −1/α < 0, the location μ − σ and the scale σ/α
μ − X is Weibull(α, σ)

name: Censored observations
convention: T is the lifetime and C is the censoring time. T and C are independent. Right censoring observes Y = min(T, C) and δ = 1{T ≤ C}. Left censoring observes Y = max(T, C) and δ = 1{T ≥ C}. C can be a random variable, a parameter or a number. The model line "censoring: right T by C" (or "left") defines the names T_obs = Y and T_event = δ. For a variable X the names are X_obs and X_event.
pdf: \text{right: } f_{Y,\delta}(y, 1) = f_T(y)\,S_C(y), \quad f_{Y,\delta}(y, 0) = g_C(y)\,S_T(y); \qquad \text{left: } f_{Y,\delta}(y, 1) = f_T(y)\,F_C(y), \quad f_{Y,\delta}(y, 0) = g_C(y)\,F_T(y)

params.name: T
params.domain: \text{a lifetime law with the density } f_T, \text{ the CDF } F_T \text{ and the survival function } S_T

params.name: C
params.domain: \text{a censoring time independent of } T, \text{ with the density } g_C, \text{ the CDF } F_C \text{ and } S_C; \ \text{or a constant } c

limits: C = ∞: complete data. Y = T and δ = 1.
C = c, a constant: Type I censoring. Y = min(T, c) has an atom of mass S_T(c) at c.
Exponential T with the rate λ and exponential C with the rate κ: Y is exponential with the rate λ + κ, and P(δ = 1) = λ/(λ + κ).
Under right censoring P(Y > t) = S_T(t) S_C(t). Thus the fraction of observed times above t estimates S_T(t) S_C(t), not S_T(t).
The Kaplan–Meier estimator is the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimate of S_T under independent right censoring. It identifies S_T only up to the largest time with S_C > 0.
If C depends on T (informative censoring), S_T is not identifiable from (Y, δ) alone.

moments.existence: Under right censoring Y ≤ T and Y ≤ C, so E[Y^r] ≤ min(E[T^r], E[C^r]) for nonnegative T and C. A fixed censoring time c bounds Y by c, so all moments of Y exist even when T has none. The MGF of Y then exists for every t. Under left censoring Y ≥ T and Y ≥ C, and E[Y^r] ≤ E[T^r] + E[C^r]. P(δ = 1) = ∫ f_T(y) S_C(y) dy under right censoring.

transforms.mgf: M_Y(t) = 1 + t\int_0^\infty e^{ty}\,S_T(y)\,S_C(y)\,dy \ (\text{right censoring, nonnegative } T, C, \text{ where the integral is finite})

links.relation: a common law of lifetimes T in censored reliability tests
a standard law of times to an event in trials, and of concentrations left-censored by a detection limit
with exponential T, the maximum likelihood estimate of the rate from censored data is the number of events divided by the total time observed
truncation removes the values outside the limit, and censoring keeps a bound for them

name: Finite mixture
convention: With probability w_j, X comes from the law F with the parameters θ_j, for j = 1, …, k. The model text names the family: mixture_poisson(w = [0.7, 0.3], lambda = [2, 9]). Each parameter of F is a vector with one entry for each component, or one number that all components share. The weights add to 1. The page does not show the component of a draw. Θ_F is the parameter domain of F.
pmf: \mathbb{P}(X \in A) = \sum_{j=1}^{k} w_j\, \mathbb{P}_{\theta_j}(X \in A), \quad p(x) = \sum_j w_j\, p_{\theta_j}(x) \ \text{or} \ f(x) = \sum_j w_j\, f_{\theta_j}(x)
limits: k = 1, or one weight equal to 1, gives the law F itself.
Components with the same parameters merge: their weights add.
A Poisson component with λ = 0 is a point mass at 0, so mixture_poisson(w = [w0, 1 − w0], lambda = [0, λ]) is the zero-inflated Poisson law.
A mixture over a continuous law of the parameter is not a finite mixture. An example is the gamma mixture of Poisson laws, the negative binomial law.
Different weights and parameters can give the same mixture law. The labels of the components can change places, so the data identify the components only up to a permutation.

moments.existence: E|X|^r is finite if and only if E|X|^r is finite for every component with a positive weight. The variance is the mean of the component variances plus the variance of the component means (the law of total variance). Thus a mixture of Poisson laws has a variance at least its mean, and above it when the component means differ.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = \sum_j w_j M_j(t), \ \text{finite where every } M_j(t) \text{ with } w_j > 0 \text{ is finite}

links.relation: a mixture of Poisson laws with different means has a variance above its mean
the gamma mixture of Poisson laws, a mixture over infinitely many components
a mixture of normal laws can give several modes and heavier shoulders
a kernel density model is the equal-weight mixture of normal laws centred at the data

name: Compound Poisson
convention: S = Y_1 + … + Y_N, with N ~ Poisson(freq) and Y_1, Y_2, … i.i.d. from the law F of a term, independent of N. S = 0 when N = 0. The model text names the law of the terms, and λ is freq. Thus compound_geometric(freq = 12, p = 0.4) has geometric terms. compound_poisson(freq = 3, lambda = 2) has Poisson terms: the Neyman type A law. The terms take values in [0, ∞). Integer terms give a law on {0, 1, 2, …}. Continuous terms give a law on [0, ∞) with an atom at 0.
pmf: \mathbb{P}(S = 0) = e^{-\lambda(1 - f_0)}, \quad \mathbb{P}(S = s) = \frac{\lambda}{s} \sum_{j=1}^{s} j\, f_j\, \mathbb{P}(S = s - j) \ \ (\text{Panjer, terms on } \{0, 1, 2, \dots\})
limits: Terms equal to 1 give S = N, the Poisson law itself.
freq = 0 gives the point mass at 0.
Poisson terms give the Neyman type A law, and geometric terms give the Pólya–Aeppli law.
As λ = freq → ∞, (S − λE[Y])/√(λE[Y²]) converges in law to N(0, 1) when E[Y²] < ∞.
With a subexponential term law, P(S > x) ~ λ P(Y > x) as x → ∞: one large term makes a large total.

moments.existence: For λ > 0, E[S^r] is finite if and only if E[Y^r] is finite. Thus a term law with a heavy tail gives S the same tail order. The MGF of S is finite exactly where the MGF of Y is finite.

links.relation: the number of terms is Poisson, and terms equal to 1 give the Poisson law
geometric terms give the Pólya–Aeppli law of clustered counts

name: Empirical discrete law
convention: The law that puts the mass w_i / Σw on each observed value x_i. Equal weights (w = 1) give each of n observations the mass 1/n. Counts as weights give the same law for grouped data. Equal values add their masses. A draw from it is a draw with replacement from the data, which is the resampling step of the ordinary bootstrap. The parameter w is a weight for each value, or one number for equal weights.
limits: One distinct value gives a point mass.
With n i.i.d. observations of a law F, the empirical CDF converges to F uniformly, almost surely (Glivenko–Cantelli).
The law gives no value outside [min x_i, max x_i], so it says nothing about the tail beyond the data.
On the integers 1 … k, the empirical law is a categorical law with p_j = w_j / Σw.

moments.existence: All moments exist: the law has finitely many values. The variance divides by Σw, not Σw − 1. It is the variance of this law, not an unbiased estimate for the law that made the data. A finite variance here does not show that the law of the data has one.

links.relation: the empirical law on the labels 1 … k is a categorical law
the kernel density model spreads each value of the empirical law with a normal kernel

name: Kernel density model
convention: X = x_J + hZ: J picks an observation with probability w_J / Σw, and Z ~ N(0, 1) is independent of J. The bandwidth h is the standard deviation of the Gaussian kernel. The density is the kernel density estimate of the data, which the model uses as a law. The parameter w is a weight for each value, or one number for equal weights.
limits: h → 0 gives the empirical law of the data.
One observation gives N(x_1, h²).
As h → ∞, the law spreads without bound, and its standardised law tends to N(0, 1).
Let the data be i.i.d. from a density f, with h → 0 and nh → ∞. Then the estimate converges to f at each point of continuity. The mean squared error is smallest for h of the order n^(−1/5).
Silverman's rule of thumb gives h = 0.9 min(s, IQR/1.34) n^(−1/5).

moments.variance: s_w^2 + h^2, \quad s_w^2 = \frac{\sum_i w_i (x_i - \bar x_w)^2}{\sum_i w_i}
moments.existence: All moments exist, and the MGF is finite for all real t: the law is a finite mixture of normal laws. The kernel adds h² to the variance, so a large bandwidth spreads the law. Values outside the range of the data, and negative values for positive data, have a positive probability.

transforms.mgf: M(t) = e^{h^2 t^2 / 2} \sum_i \frac{w_i}{\sum w}\, e^{t x_i}
transforms.cf: \varphi(t) = e^{-h^2 t^2 / 2} \sum_i \frac{w_i}{\sum w}\, e^{i t x_i}

links.relation: the limit h → 0 of the kernel density model
each kernel is N(x_i, h²)
an equal-weight finite mixture of normal laws

name: Truncated law
convention: X has the law F conditioned on lower ≤ X ≤ upper. The model text names F: truncated_poisson(lambda = 2, lower = 1, upper = inf). Values outside [lower, upper] do not occur at all: no record of them exists. The kept mass Z = P_F(lower ≤ X ≤ upper) must be positive.
pmf: f_t(x) = \frac{f(x)}{Z}\, \mathbf{1}\{\ell \le x \le u\}, \quad F_t(x) = \frac{F(x) - F(\ell^-)}{Z}, \quad Z = F(u) - F(\ell^-)
limits: lower = −∞ and upper = ∞ give F itself.
The zero-truncated Poisson law has the mean λ/(1 − e^(−λ)).
A geometric law truncated below at b is b plus a geometric law: the geometric law has no memory.
Truncation differs from censoring. Censoring keeps a bound for each value outside the limit. Truncation keeps no record of it.

moments.existence: A bounded interval [lower, upper] keeps all moments. An unbounded side keeps the tail order of F on that side, so a heavy right tail stays heavy after truncation from below.

transforms.mgf: M_t(t) = \frac{1}{Z}\, \mathbb{E}_F\left[e^{tX} \mathbf{1}\{\ell \le X \le u\}\right], \ \text{finite for all } t \ \text{on a bounded interval}

links.relation: the zero-truncated Poisson law of counts that are at least 1
truncation from below gives a shifted geometric law, because the law has no memory
censoring keeps a bound for each value outside the limit, and truncation keeps no record
